prediction:
THOUGHT: The patient is a 62-year-old male with a positive fecal occult blood test (FOBT) on routine screening, no gastrointestinal symptoms, and a first-degree family history of large intestinal (colorectal) cancer—specifically, his father died of it. This elevates his risk for colorectal neoplasia. Colonoscopy—appropriately indicated given the positive FOBT and family history—revealed a single polyp in the descending colon, which was excised. Histopathology shows a tubular adenoma with 75% tubular architecture and no high-grade dysplasia. Tubular adenomas are the most common type of precancerous colorectal polyps; they are benign but carry malignant potential proportional to size, degree of dysplasia, and villous component. The absence of high-grade dysplasia and the purely tubular (i.e., low-risk) histology indicate a low-risk adenoma. Importantly, the diagnosis is not “colorectal cancer” (no invasive carcinoma identified), nor is it “inflammatory bowel disease” or “diverticulosis” (no supporting evidence). The clinical scenario centers on the identification and characterization of a premalignant lesion in an asymptomatic, average- to increased-risk individual. Per current guidelines (e.g., USPSTF, ACG, ASGE), this finding is classified as an adenomatous polyp—specifically, a low-risk tubular adenoma.

DIAGNOSIS: Tubular adenoma of the colon
